A task must not show as finished while work its run started in the background
is still going. Right now a Claude Code task that starts a shell command in
the background (run_in_background, e.g. a long `cargo build`) and then ends
its turn to wait for it is marked finished: Claude Code emits a `result` when
the turn ends, and the harness takes that result as the last one, because the
only background work it waits on is subagents (`task_started` with
`task_type: local_agent`). The task closes, its input is closed so it can't be
fed more, and the build carries on unseen. When the build ends, the harness
would have woken the agent to act on it, but the task is already over.

What should be true afterwards:

1. Background work of any kind holds the run open. The run keeps the set of
   Claude Code background tasks that have started and not yet ended, whatever
   their task_type (local_agent, local_bash, or any kind added later):
   `system` `task_started` adds its task_id, and `task_notification` for that
   id removes it, whatever its status. `task_notification` doesn't say its
   kind, so ids are matched against those seen starting.

2. A result only ends the run once every message sent has been taken in AND
   no background task is still going. A result that comes while any is still
   going is an answer (Answered, as a result is today while a subagent is
   running): the task stays running, its input stays open, and it can still
   be fed. The run ends on the first result after the last background task
   has ended.

3. The Subagents panel is unchanged: it still lists only local_agent tasks.
   Background shell tasks hold the run open but aren't shown as subagents.

4. A task isn't shown as finished until the harness process has exited as
   well as having given its last result. If a last result has come but the
   process is still running, the task stays running until it exits, then
   finishes in the state of that last result. A process that exits with no
   result finishes as it does today.

5. Stopping a task still ends it straight away, background work and all
   (its whole process group is killed), whatever is still running.

Spec: the rule for when a run ends is in the harness-integration scope's
feeding paragraph ("A result no longer ends the task on its own: the run ends
with a result once every message sent has been taken in ..."), and the
subagents rule in the right sidebar's subagents component. Update those rather
than adding parallel anchors, and make the harness-integration scope say that
background tasks of every kind, not only subagents, hold the run open.

Code: src/harness.rs — Messages (rename `subagents` to something like
`background`, holding every started task id), Messages::read, Feed::read
(input closed only on the real last result), and the run loop / Stop::wait,
so the task finishes on process exit after the last result. subagent_event
stays as it is for the panel. Update the tests: the existing one that says a
background shell starts no subagent should still pass, and add tests that a
result while a local_bash task is running is Answered and keeps input open,
that the result after its task_notification is Finished, and that a task
whose last result has come doesn't finish until its process exits.

# Piton Fluency

This is a working reference for Piton, the Belay framework bundled with it, the
project configuration, the package manager and the tooling. Read it before you
read or change a Piton specbase. It is generated from the specification in
`spec/` by the GenerateFluencyPrompt skill. Where the compiler behaves

## 1. What Piton is, and why

Piton is a declarative, whitespace-structured language for writing agent
guidance: skills, agents, commands, scoped instructions and reference
documents. Its author calls it a "semi-natural programming language". Prose and
structure are both first-class. A value can be a paragraph of plain English or
a typed, inherited, composed data structure, and most files mix the two.

The founding thesis (`spec/scope/founding-thesis/`) explains the design:

- Every programming language is an abstraction over the layer beneath it. Once
  an abstraction is accepted, nobody cares how its compiled output is produced,
  as long as the output is good. Agentic development is the next step in that
  history. In this model the agent is the compiler.
- Humans are good at designing coherent systems, not at typing out the latest
  accepted abstraction. Piton keeps the describing, constraining and thinking,
  and hands the manual labour to the agent.
- Prompting an agent session by session produces results that live in one
  developer's memory and cannot be traced. AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and Markdown
  skills help, but pure prose decays. It is ambiguous, it gets duplicated, and
  it has no tools for reuse. Piton adds imports, inheritance, types and
  references to prose, while keeping prose for the things prose says best
  ("the button should be blue with contrasting text"). Plain prompting is fine
  for a small one-off tool. A sufficiently complex system needs a traceable
  artifact of the process itself, not just its output, and more so when
  several people work on it.
- The real problem is repetition. Much software work is the same patterns
  again (CRUD APIs, layouts, navigation bars, modal forms). Functions, classes
  and generics are ways of wrapping a problem once it becomes a pattern. The
  aim is to keep designing systems and stop typing the patterns: "I never
  wanted to write code itself; I wanted to create."
- The CNC analogy: G-code replaced the machinist's hand, and CAM then sat on
  top of G-code by combining design intent with the machinist's expertise. The
  CAM engineer never types G-code but is essential. CNC did not replace most of
  the machinist's skill, and two jobs (engineer, machinist) became three (plus
  the CAM engineer). The Piton author plays that role for agents.
- The stated goal is that you can paste the specification into an agentic
  coding tool and get a compiler for Piton and Belay back. This repository is
  that experiment. The specification in `spec/` is written in Piton, and the
  compiler in `crates/` is judged against it.

Core facts:

- **There is no runtime.** Piton compiles to data (JSON, YAML, Markdown)
  through **renderers**. Frameworks such as Belay add **adapters** on top of
  the renderers. There are no functions, no loops, and no conditionals except
  the ternary operator. Every value is immutable.
- **The `.pi` source is the source of truth.** Compiled Markdown under
  `.claude/reference`, `.claude/skills`, `CLAUDE.md` files and so on is derived
  output. Make lasting changes in the `.pi` files and rebuild. Never hand-edit
  generated artifacts.
- A **specbase** is a Piton project: a `piton.config.pi`, a source root
  (usually `spec/`), an entry file, and the frameworks and packages it uses.
- **Successful compilation shows that the guidance is well-formed. It does not
  show that an agent will behave correctly.** Artifact generation is
  predictable, but agent behaviour is probabilistic.

## 2. Files, whitespace, comments, keywords

- Source files use the `.pi` extension. A directory that contains an
  `index.pi` is a module (section 7.2).
- **Indentation defines structure**, as in Python. Tabs or any number of
  spaces are accepted, but one file must be consistent. The canonical style is
  4 spaces. `piton format` enforces it, and it cannot be configured.
- **Comments** are line-only and start with `//`. There are no block comments.
  **A comment has to be on its own line.** After code, `//` is just text, so
  `url: https://example.com // note` is the string
  `https://example.com // note`. The formatter adds one space after `//` when
  there is none and touches nothing else in the comment, so commented-out code
  keeps its spacing. To start a value with `//`, escape it:
  `\ // \ Just Text`.
- **Reserved words** have special meaning:

  ```
  anchor abstract export from import use as extends pass
  this self super
  true false null
  any simple complex
  string number boolean list dictionary
  ```

  You can't use them as your own keywords (`reserved-keyword`), but **you can
  use them as keys**. As keys they are just strings: `null: text`,
  `use: text` and `as: text` are ordinary properties.
- **Keywords** are all lowercase and may be kebab-case
  (`arithmetic-operator`). Users define their own with `as` (section 8.6).
- **`pass`** fills the body of an anchor that has no properties of its own. An
  anchor always needs something indented under it; `anchor X:` with nothing
  under it is `empty-anchor`.

  ```piton
  anchor Child extends Base:
      pass
  ```

## 3. Declarations and values

A file is a sequence of top-level declarations. Top-level names are variables
scoped to their file: they are global within the file and invisible outside it
unless exported.

```piton
myVariable: 42
export pi: 3.14

export anchor MyAnchor:
    description: This is my anchor
```

`key: value` assigns a value, and the space after the colon is required. The
value can sit on the same line or be indented on the lines below:

```piton
sameLine: Hello, World!
nextLine:
    Hello, World!
```

Both produce `"Hello, World!"`. The leading indentation belongs to the syntax,
not to the string.

**A property has to have a value.** A name with nothing after it and nothing
indented under it is a compiler error (`empty-value`). If you mean nothing,
write `null`. The one exception is a required property in an abstract anchor
(`title:: string`); anywhere else a constraint with no value is
`missing-value`.

### 3.1 Types

Piton is loosely typed, with optional constraints.

| Type | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `string` | Unicode text. Never quoted (section 3.3). |
| `number` | One numeric type, a 64-bit IEEE 754 float, with no int/float distinction. |
| `boolean` | Lowercase `true` and `false`. |
| `null` | Lowercase `null`. It is the only "nothing" value (there is no `undefined`), and `{null == null}` is `true`. |
| `list` | An ordered collection. Item types may be mixed unless a constraint says otherwise. |
| `dictionary` | Key/value pairs. Keys are strings, and value types may be mixed unless constrained. |
| anchor | The one user-defined type (section 8). |

- **Simple types** are string, number, boolean and null.
- **Complex types** are list, dictionary and anchor.
- A **reference** is its own type, produced by `@{}` (section 6.5). It points
  at an anchor or a property on one instead of copying it.

- **Inference.** An unconstrained variable or property can hold any type,
  inferred from how the value looks: `true` is a boolean but `true story` is
  a string; `42` and `-42` are numbers but `42 things` is a string; `A + B`
  and `This costs $5 + tax` are strings (no braces, no expression); `null` is
  null; `"false"` is a string; `${a + b}` is always a string.

Every built-in type is described by an anchor that uses the abstract `type`
keyword (`spec/scope/language/types/lib/Type.pi`). A `type` anchor provides a
`description` (simple or complex) and its `supportedOperators` (a list of
operators, or null). Using an operator a type does not list is a compiler
error, but the compiler applies the coercion (4.2) and inference rules before
it reports one:

| Type | Supported operators |
| --- | --- |
| number | arithmetic `+ - * / %`, comparison `== != < <= > >=` |
| string | concatenation `+`, `++`, comparison `== != < <= > >=` |
| boolean | logical `&& \|\| !`, `==`, `!=` |
| null | `==`, `!=` |
| list | merge `+`, `++`, `==`, `!=` |
| dictionary | `.`, merge `+`, `++`, `==`, `!=` |
| anchor | `.`, `==`, `!=` |
| reference | `==`, `!=` |

### 3.2 Numbers

```piton
myInt: 123
myFloat: 3.14
mySmallFloat: 0.14
myBigNumber: 1_200_000.00
negative: -5
```

- **A decimal needs its leading `0`.** `0.14` is a number; `.5` is not a number
  (unconstrained, it is the string `".5"`).
- `_` may separate digits for readability.
- **There is no exponent notation.** `1e3` is not a number (unconstrained, it
  is silently the string `"1e3"`, not an error).
- A negative number is written with a minus, like `-5`. A list item always has
  a space after its dash, so `-5` is a number and `- 5` is a list item.
- **The minus is only part of a number.** There's no minus in front of an
  expression: `{-price}` is an error. Write `{0 - price}`.
- Compiled numbers take their shortest form: `1_200_000.00` becomes `1200000`
  and `0.50` becomes `0.5`.

### 3.3 Strings and quotes

- Strings are not quoted. **Quotes are ordinary characters in a value**, so
  `greeting: "Hello"` is the string `"Hello"`, quotes and all, and
  `"false"` is a string with quotes in it, never a boolean.
- The one exception is inside an expression, where bare words are symbols, so
  string operands are written in double quotes: `{"Hello" + name}`. There the
  quotes are not part of the string.
- In a multi-line block, consecutive lines join with one space. **A blank line
  starts a new paragraph**, which compiles to a line break (`\n`). Several
  blank lines in a row still count as one.

  ```piton
  myString:
      This broken string is not considered
      a line break.

      While this *is* a new paragraph because there was a blank line above.
  ```

  This compiles to
  `"This broken string is not considered a line break.\nWhile this *is* a new paragraph because there was a blank line above."`.

- **Markdown in a string is plain text.** Piton has no link syntax, so
  `[the guide](./guide.md)` and `![A diagram](./diagram.png)` pass through
  exactly as written. Nothing resolves, rewrites or checks them, and they are
  never an error. The only links Piton makes are `@{}` references.

### 3.4 Escaping

Escaping works by wrapping. Put backslashes around the special characters,
with a space on each side. The spaces are part of the wrapper and are removed:
`\ {1 + 2 + 3} \` compiles to the literal `{1 + 2 + 3}`. It is the only way to
escape, and even a single character gets wrapped: `\ : \` gives `:`.

- **Stacking.** To escape backslashes themselves, use more of them. The
  closing wrapper must match the opening one, so anything inside can use fewer:
  `\\ \ {x} \ \\` compiles to `\ {x} \`.
- **Multi-line escape blocks.** A line holding only backslashes opens a block,
  and a line with the same number of backslashes closes it. Everything in
  between is kept exactly, line breaks and indentation included. The spec uses
  three backslashes (`\\\`) for these.
- **Code fences are ordinary text.** A ```` ``` ```` fence does not protect
  anything: expressions, comments, list items and keys inside it are still
  parsed. So put an escape block inside the fence, the way every example in the
  spec does:

  ````piton
  description:
      ```piton
      \\\
      anchor Example:
          value: {1 + 2}
      \\\
      ```
  ````

  This keeps the fence and the example exactly as written. Markdown tables
  need the same treatment, because otherwise their rows join into one line.

**Prose pitfalls.** Each of these silently changes the structure of a string
block:

- A line that starts `- ` makes a list item, and a line that starts `+ ` or
  `++ ` makes a composition line (section 5). A property declared `:: string`
  then fails. Escape the start: `\ - \ item`.
- A line shaped like `word: text` (`Similarly: ...`, `Inputs: none`, or a
  wrapped line that happens to start with `type:`) becomes a dictionary key,
  and the block turns into an implicit list. Escape the colon (`\ : \`) or
  rewrap the paragraph.
- Backticks do not protect anything. `` `{x}` `` is still an expression, and
  `` `a + b` `` in a table cell is text only because it has no braces.
- An expression in running text changes the value's shape when it evaluates
  to a list, dictionary or anchor (section 6.2).

Wrapping stops text being parsed as syntax, but it doesn't change the inferred
type: `\ false \` is still the boolean `false`. To get the string, write
`${false}`.

The wrapper is the only way to escape. A backslash that doesn't open a
wrapper (a backslash followed by a space) is just a backslash, so `\:` is the
two characters `\:`. Write `\ : \` to escape a colon.

### 3.5 Lists

```piton
markdownStyle:
    - One
    - List
    - Item

inlineStyle: [This, is, a, list, of, strings]

nestedMarkdownList:
    - Level 1
        - Level 2
            - Level 3
```

`nestedMarkdownList` is `[Level 1, [Level 2, [Level 3]]]`.

- **Items cannot be accessed by index.** By design there is no `myList[0]`.
  Piton describes things; it does not compute them, and lists exist to be
  merged and inherited.
- **A list item is never a key**, even with a colon at the end. `- Settings:`
  is just the string `"Settings:"`.
- **Anything indented under a list item is not part of that item.** It becomes
  the next item in the list, so a dictionary indented under an item is its own
  item, right after it:

  ```piton
  repos:
      - https://github.com/piton-lang/piton-rs
          tag: v1
      - https://github.com/piton-lang/other
  ```

  This compiles to
  `["https://github.com/piton-lang/piton-rs", {"tag": "v1"}, "https://github.com/piton-lang/other"]`.
  A dictionary that ends up as an item of an explicit list cannot be addressed.

### 3.6 Dictionaries

A dictionary has one syntax, which is indentation:

```piton
firstLevel:
    secondLevel:
        thirdLevel: This is a string
```

- Dot access works: `{firstLevel.secondLevel.thirdLevel}` gives
  `"This is a string"`.
- **Valid keys** contain Unicode letters, Unicode digits, `_` and `-`, and
  nothing else (no spaces, no dots). Keys are always strings, even when they
  look like something else, so `thisIsAKey`, `123`, `foo-bar`, `false` and
  `null` are valid keys, while `This is a key` and `a.b` are not.
- **A hyphen inside a name is part of the name.** `{config.foo-bar}` reads the
  key `foo-bar`. For subtraction, put spaces around the minus: `{a - b}`.
- A list indented under a key is that key's value. If the key also has
  something above the list, like text or another dictionary, the value becomes
  an implicit list (3.7) and the list goes in as one item:

  ```piton
  plain:
      - x
      - y
  mixed:
      text
      - x
      - y
  ```

  `plain` is `["x", "y"]`; `mixed` is `["text", ["x", "y"]]`.

### 3.7 Implicit lists

A block that mixes prose, list items and keys becomes an **implicit list**
that keeps the source order:

```piton
combined:
    This is a string

    - This
    - Is
    - A
    - List

    nestedDictionary:
        deeplyNestedDictionary: This is a string
```

This compiles to
`["This is a string", ["This", "Is", "A", "List"], {"nestedDictionary": {"deeplyNestedDictionary": "This is a string"}}]`.

- **Keys declared directly in the mixed block stay addressable.**
  `{combined.nestedDictionary.deeplyNestedDictionary}` still resolves.
- The prose and list elements cannot be addressed, because there is no list
  access.
- An expression in running text that gives a list, dictionary or anchor also
  makes an implicit list (section 6.2).

## 4. Variables and type constraints

- A variable is declared by naming it at the top level of a file:
  `myVariable: 42`.
- The file is its scope. `export` makes it visible to other files.
- **Inside an expression, a plain name always means a variable from the file
  (or something imported), even inside an anchor.** To reach a property on the
  anchor you are in, use `this` or `self`:

  ```piton
  x: top-level

  anchor Card:
      x: card
      fromFile: {x}
      fromCard: {this.x}
  ```

  `Card.fromFile` is `"top-level"` and `Card.fromCard` is `"card"`.
- Everything is immutable. There is no compile-time mutability.

### 4.1 Constraint syntax

A constraint is written `name:: type: value`. **The whitespace after `::` and
after `:` is mandatory**, so `myVariable::number:42` is an error
(`constraint-spacing`), in blocks as well as at the top level.

```piton
count:: number: 42
tags:: string[]: [foo, bar, baz]
config:: dictionary:
    a:: number: 1
    b:: string: foo
a:: complex: [1, 2, 3]
c:: simple: 1
g:: any: 1
h:: any:
    - String
    - [1, 2, 3]
```

- `simple` accepts string, number, boolean or null. `complex` accepts list,
  dictionary or anchor. `any` accepts anything.
- `T[]` is a list of `T`, for any type, including anchor types (`Foo[]`).
- `extends Foo[]` (or `extends Foo`) accepts anything that inherits from the
  anchor `Foo` (section 8.4). You can use it anywhere, but it is most at home
  in abstracts. The spec also uses it on exported lists:
  `export ARITHMETIC_OPERATORS:: extends ArithmeticOperator[]: ...`.
- An anchor-typed constraint (`f:: Foo: {Foo}`) is satisfied by the anchor or a
  copy of it (section 6.1).
- A file that names an abstract as a type must import it with
  `from ./Foo import Foo`. `use` alone is not enough (section 7.3).

### 4.2 Multiple constraints and coercion

Coercion is intentionally limited. With several constraints, they are tried
**left to right** and the first type the value can validly represent wins.

```piton
first:: number:: string: 42
second:: string:: number: 42
written:: string: 1.0
evaluated:: string: {1.0}
quoted:: boolean:: number:: string: "false"
```

- `first` is the number `42`; `second` is the string `"42"`.
- **A literal keeps its text when coerced to a string.** `written` is
  `"1.0"`. An expression is evaluated first and its result is coerced, so
  `evaluated` is `"1"`.
- `quoted` is the string `"false"`, quotes and all, because quotes are
  ordinary characters and `"false"` is not a boolean.
- **Booleans and null are never coerced**, to strings or anything else. `flag:: string: false`
  is a compiler error (`type-mismatch`), not the string `"false"`. If you want
  the string, write `${false}`.
- Lists, dictionaries and anchors are never coerced into unrelated types.
- If no constraint accepts the value, compilation fails with `type-mismatch`.
- These rules are about constraints. Operators such as `+` have their own
  rules (section 6.4).

### 4.3 Required and optional properties

In an abstract anchor:

```piton
abstract anchor Card:
    title:: string
    subtitle:: string:: null
    footer:: string:: null: null

anchor MyCard extends Card:
    title: Hello
    subtitle: null
```

- A constraint with no value is **required**. Anything that extends the anchor
  has to give it a value (`unimplemented-property` otherwise). Adding `null` to
  the constraint lets that value be null, but it still has to be written, so
  `title` and `subtitle` are required.
- A property with a default value is **optional**. The usual way to write one
  is to allow null and default to null, like `footer`. `x:: string:: null: null`
  gives `null`. The language server does not complain about a missing
  optional property.
- **A child can't redeclare a constraint it inherits**, only give it a value.
  If `subtitle` is already constrained, `subtitle: Hi` is fine and
  `subtitle:: string: Hi` is `redeclared-constraint`.

## 5. Composition lines inside blocks

**Blocks are built from top to bottom. A line that starts with `+` or `++`
takes everything above it and combines it with that line's value**, using the
operator of the same name (section 6.4).

```piton
anchor BaseAnchor:
    items:
        - A
        - B
        - C

anchor ChildAnchor extends BaseAnchor:
    items:
        + {super.items}
        - D
        - E
        - F
```

`ChildAnchor.items` is `[A, B, C, D, E, F]`: the block starts empty, the `+`
brings in `super.items`, then D, E and F are added. Without the `+`
(`- {super.items}`) the result is `[[A, B, C], D, E, F]`.

- On lists, `+` merges and **removes duplicates, keeping the last
  occurrence**. Items `A, B, C, D` followed by `+ {super.items}` give
  `[D, A, B, C]`.
- On lists, `++` keeps everything: items `A, B, C, D` followed by
  `++ {super.items}` give `[A, B, C, D, A, B, C]`.
- On dictionaries, `+` is a shallow merge and `++` a deep merge.
- **On strings, `+` joins with nothing in between and `++` joins with a line
  break:**

  ```piton
  anchor Base:
      d: Base text.

  anchor Plus extends Base:
      d:
          Child text.
          + {super.d}

  anchor DoublePlus extends Base:
      d:
          Child text.
          ++ {super.d}
  ```

  `Plus.d` is `"Child text.Base text."` and `DoublePlus.d` is
  `"Child text.\nBase text."`.
- A block holding only `+ {x}` is the same as `{x}`.
- To put inherited prose in front with a space, interpolate instead:
  `${super.description} and more from the child.`

## 6. Expressions

**Nothing is evaluated unless it is in braces.** `a + b` is the string
`"a + b"`, and `{a + b}` is `3` when `a` is 1 and `b` is 2. The braces keep the
compiler simple, and they mean an unrecognized word never silently falls back
to being a string.

- Inside the braces, **bare words are symbols**. Quote string operands:
  `{2 + "Hello"}` gives `"2Hello"`. An unknown name is `unresolved-symbol`.
  List literals inside braces follow the same rule: `{["A", "B"] + ["C"]}`.
- **Keep the whole expression inside the braces.** `{this.flag && false}`
  evaluates; `{this.flag} && false` is text around an expression.
- **Braces that don't hold a valid expression are an error**, and so is an
  empty `{}` or `${}`. To write braces as text, escape them: `\ {1 +} \`.
- **Forward references resolve.** Unresolved references are errors, and so are
  cyclic values: `A: {B}` together with `B: {A}` fails with `cyclic-value`.
- Collections are copied by value:

  ```piton
  myList: [1, 2, 3]
  myDictionary:
      list: {myList}
  newList: {myDictionary.list + [4, 5, 6]}
  ```

  `newList` is `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`.
- **Anchors are copied too, but the copy still knows which anchor it is.** If
  `x` is `{Foo}`, then `{x == Foo}` is `true`, `${x}` is `"Foo"`, and `x`
  passes a `Foo` type constraint. The output is still a copy of Foo's content.
  For a link instead of a copy, use `@{Foo}`.

### 6.1 The four expression forms

| Form | Name | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `{expr}` | Standard | The intrinsic value with its type preserved. An anchor serializes as its resolved content (a copy that keeps its identity). |
| `${expr}` | String | Converts the result to a string. |
| `#{expr}` | Numeric | Converts the result to a number. |
| `@{expr}` | Reference | A reference to an anchor or a property on one. Renders as a link or path, never as the content. |

Use `@{X}` to point at another document, `{X}` to embed a copy of it, and
`${X}` to mention it by name.

### 6.2 Expressions in text

If the whole value is one expression (`total: {a + b}`), it keeps its type. If
there is other text around it:

- `${x}` turns the result into a string, so the whole value is a string.
- `{x}` with a simple value drops it into the text: `Total: {a + b}` is
  `"Total: 3"`.
- `{x}` with a list, dictionary or anchor copies it in and **turns the
  property into an implicit list**. `See {Foo} for details` becomes a list of
  `"See"`, a copy of Foo, and `"for details"`.
- `@{x}` puts in a reference, which ends up as a link or a path.

### 6.3 Conversions

`${}` (string):

- A string is returned unchanged. A number becomes its text form. A boolean
  becomes `true` or `false`. Null becomes `null`.
- An anchor becomes its name as written in the source: `${Child}` gives
  `"Child"`, and `${self}` gives the name of the current most-derived anchor.
  It is not turned into a title.
- A named list or dictionary becomes its name: `Anchor.propertyName`, or just
  the variable name at the top of a file. So if `tags` is a top-level list,
  `${tags}` is `"tags"`.
- A list or dictionary with no name (`${[1, 2]}`) is `no-string-form`.
- **`${}` never pulls in the contents** of a list, dictionary or anchor, only
  its name. For the contents use `{x}`; for a link use `@{x}`. In
  `Metadata.pi`:

  ```piton
  export anchor Metadata:
      name: Piton
      version:: string: 1.0

  export byName: Information about Piton ${Metadata}
  export byValue: Information about Piton {Metadata}
  export byLink: Information about Piton @{Metadata}
  ```

  `byName` is `"Information about Piton Metadata"`, `byValue` is
  `["Information about Piton", {"name": "Piton", "version": "1.0"}]`, and
  `byLink` is `"Information about Piton ./Metadata.json:Metadata"` (in
  Markdown, `[Metadata](./Metadata.md#metadata)`).
- The result is never re-parsed as source.
- In structured output the value stays a string; whatever escaping the output
  format needs is applied when it is serialized.

`#{}` (numeric):

- A number is returned unchanged. A string converts only if the **entire**
  string is a valid Piton numeric literal: `#{"42"}` gives `42`. It is never
  evaluated as an expression.
- Booleans, null, collections and anchors are rejected (`not-a-number`).
- The result is a number you can keep computing with. In structured output it
  stays numeric; it becomes text only when the output format needs text.

### 6.4 Operators

| Group | Operators | Rules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access | `.` | Property access on dictionaries and anchors. |
| Arithmetic | `+ - * / %` | Numbers only. Division or modulo by zero is an error. `%` keeps the sign of the left side: `{-7 % 3}` is `-1`. |

18	## 1. What Piton is, and why
19	
20	Piton is a declarative, whitespace-structured language for writing agent
21	guidance: skills, agents, commands, scoped instructions and reference
22	documents. Its author calls it a "semi-natural programming language". Prose and
23	structure are both first-class. A value can be a paragraph of plain English or
24	a typed, inherited, composed data structure, and most files mix the two.
25	
26	The founding thesis (`spec/scope/founding-thesis/`) explains the design:
27	
28	- Every programming language is an abstraction over the layer beneath it. Once
29	  an abstraction is accepted, nobody cares how its compiled output is produced,
30	  as long as the output is good. Agentic development is the next step in that
31	  history. In this model the agent is the compiler.
32	- Humans are good at designing coherent systems, not at typing out the latest
33	  accepted abstraction. Piton keeps the describing, constraining and thinking,
34	  and hands the manual labour to the agent.
35	- Prompting an agent session by session produces results that live in one
36	  developer's memory and cannot be traced. AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and Markdown
37	  skills help, but pure prose decays. It is ambiguous, it gets duplicated, and
38	  it has no tools for reuse. Piton adds imports, inheritance, types and
39	  references to prose, while keeping prose for the things prose says best
40	  ("the button should be blue with contrasting text"). Plain prompting is fine
41	  for a small one-off tool. A sufficiently complex system needs a traceable
42	  artifact of the process itself, not just its output, and more so when
43	  several people work on it.
44	- The real problem is repetition. Much software work is the same patterns
45	  again (CRUD APIs, layouts, navigation bars, modal forms). Functions, classes
46	  and generics are ways of wrapping a problem once it becomes a pattern. The
47	  aim is to keep designing systems and stop typing the patterns: "I never
48	  wanted to write code itself; I wanted to create."
49	- The CNC analogy: G-code replaced the machinist's hand, and CAM then sat on
50	  top of G-code by combining design intent with the machinist's expertise. The
51	  CAM engineer never types G-code but is essential. CNC did not replace most of
52	  the machinist's skill, and two jobs (engineer, machinist) became three (plus
53	  the CAM engineer). The Piton author plays that role for agents.
54	- The stated goal is that you can paste the specification into an agentic
55	  coding tool and get a compiler for Piton and Belay back. This repository is
56	  that experiment. The specification in `spec/` is written in Piton, and the
57	  compiler in `crates/` is judged against it.

59	Core facts:
60	
61	- **There is no runtime.** Piton compiles to data (JSON, YAML, Markdown)
62	  through **renderers**. Frameworks such as Belay add **adapters** on top of
63	  the renderers. There are no functions, no loops, and no conditionals except
64	  the ternary operator. Every value is immutable.
65	- **The `.pi` source is the source of truth.** Compiled Markdown under

75	## 2. Files, whitespace, comments, keywords
76	
77	- Source files use the `.pi` extension. A directory that contains an
78	  `index.pi` is a module (section 7.2).
79	- **Indentation defines structure**, as in Python. Tabs or any number of
80	  spaces are accepted, but one file must be consistent. The canonical style is
81	  4 spaces. `piton format` enforces it, and it cannot be configured.
82	- **Comments** are line-only and start with `//`. There are no block comments.
83	  **A comment has to be on its own line.** After code, `//` is just text, so
84	  `url: https://example.com // note` is the string
85	  `https://example.com // note`. The formatter adds one space after `//` when
86	  there is none and touches nothing else in the comment, so commented-out code

88	  `\ // \ Just Text`.

90

93	  this self super

95	  any simple complex

97	  ```
98

100	  use them as keys**. As keys they are just strings: `null: text`,
101	  `use: text` and `as: text` are ordinary properties.
102	- **Keywords** are all lowercase and may be kebab-case
103	  (`arithmetic-operator`). Users define their own with `as` (section 8.6).

108	  ```piton

110	      pass
111	  ```

113	## 3. Declarations and values
114	
115	A file is a sequence of top-level declarations. Top-level names are variables
116	scoped to their file: they are global within the file and invisible outside it
117	unless exported.
118	
119	```piton
120	myVariable: 42
121	export pi: 3.14
122	
123	export anchor MyAnchor:
124	    description: This is my anchor
125	```
126	
127	`key: value` assigns a value, and the space after the colon is required. The
128	value can sit on the same line or be indented on the lines below:
129	
130	```piton
131	sameLine: Hello, World!
132	nextLine:
133	    Hello, World!
134	```
135	
136	Both produce `"Hello, World!"`. The leading indentation belongs to the syntax,
137	not to the string.
138	
139	**A property has to have a value.** A name with nothing after it and nothing
140	indented under it is a compiler error (`empty-value`). If you mean nothing,
141	write `null`. The one exception is a required property in an abstract anchor
142	(`title:: string`); anywhere else a constraint with no value is

145	### 3.1 Types
146	
147	Piton is loosely typed, with optional constraints.
148	
149	| Type | Notes |
150	| --- | --- |
151	| `string` | Unicode text. Never quoted (section 3.3). |
152	| `number` | One numeric type, a 64-bit IEEE 754 float, with no int/float distinction. |
153	| `boolean` | Lowercase `true` and `false`. |
154	| `null` | Lowercase `null`. It is the only "nothing" value (there is no `undefined`), and `{null == null}` is `true`. |
155	| `list` | An ordered collection. Item types may be mixed unless a constraint says otherwise. |
156	| `dictionary` | Key/value pairs. Keys are strings, and value types may be mixed unless constrained. |

188	### 3.2 Numbers
189

192	myFloat: 3.14
193	mySmallFloat: 0.14
194	myBigNumber: 1_200_000.00
195	negative: -5
196	```

198	- **A decimal needs its leading `0`.** `0.14` is a number; `.5` is not a number
199	  (unconstrained, it is the string `".5"`).
200	- `_` may separate digits for readability.
201	- **There is no exponent notation.** `1e3` is not a number (unconstrained, it
202	  is silently the string `"1e3"`, not an error).
203	- A negative number is written with a minus, like `-5`. A list item always has

210	### 3.3 Strings and quotes
211	
212	- Strings are not quoted. **Quotes are ordinary characters in a value**, so
213	  `greeting: "Hello"` is the string `"Hello"`, quotes and all, and
214	  `"false"` is a string with quotes in it, never a boolean.

216	  string operands are written in double quotes: `{"Hello" + name}`. There the
217	  quotes are not part of the string.
218	- In a multi-line block, consecutive lines join with one space. **A blank line
219	  starts a new paragraph**, which compiles to a line break (`\n`). Several
220	  blank lines in a row still count as one.
221	
222	  ```piton
223	  myString:
224	      This broken string is not considered
225	      a line break.
226	
227	      While this *is* a new paragraph because there was a blank line above.
228	  ```
229	
230	  This compiles to
231	  `"This broken string is not considered a line break.\nWhile this *is* a new paragraph because there was a blank line above."`.
232	
233	- **Markdown in a string is plain text.** Piton has no link syntax, so
234	  `[the guide](./guide.md)` and `![A diagram](./diagram.png)` pass through
235	  exactly as written. Nothing resolves, rewrites or checks them, and they are
236	  never an error. The only links Piton makes are `@{}` references.
237	
238	### 3.4 Escaping
239	
240	Escaping works by wrapping. Put backslashes around the special characters,
241	with a space on each side. The spaces are part of the wrapper and are removed:
242	`\ {1 + 2 + 3} \` compiles to the literal `{1 + 2 + 3}`. It is the only way to
243	escape, and even a single character gets wrapped: `\ : \` gives `:`.
244	
245	- **Stacking.** To escape backslashes themselves, use more of them. The
246	  closing wrapper must match the opening one, so anything inside can use fewer:
247	  `\\ \ {x} \ \\` compiles to `\ {x} \`.
248	- **Multi-line escape blocks.** A line holding only backslashes opens a block,
249	  and a line with the same number of backslashes closes it. Everything in
250	  between is kept exactly, line breaks and indentation included. The spec uses
251	  three backslashes (`\\\`) for these.

253	  anything: expressions, comments, list items and keys inside it are still
254	  parsed. So put an escape block inside the fence, the way every example in the
255	  spec does:
256	
257	  ````piton
258	  description:
259	      ```piton
260	      \\\
261	      anchor Example:
262	          value: {1 + 2}
263	      \\\
264	      ```
265	  ````

267	  This keeps the fence and the example exactly as written. Markdown tables
268	  need the same treatment, because otherwise their rows join into one line.
269	
270	**Prose pitfalls.** Each of these silently changes the structure of a string

273	- A line that starts `- ` makes a list item, and a line that starts `+ ` or
274	  `++ ` makes a composition line (section 5). A property declared `:: string`

284	
285	Wrapping stops text being parsed as syntax, but it doesn't change the inferred
286	type: `\ false \` is still the boolean `false`. To get the string, write
287	`${false}`.
288	
289	The wrapper is the only way to escape. A backslash that doesn't open a
290	wrapper (a backslash followed by a space) is just a backslash, so `\:` is the
291	two characters `\:`. Write `\ : \` to escape a colon.
292	
293	### 3.5 Lists

295	```piton
296	markdownStyle:
297	    - One
298	    - List
299	    - Item
300	
301	inlineStyle: [This, is, a, list, of, strings]
302	
303	nestedMarkdownList:
304	    - Level 1
305	        - Level 2
306	            - Level 3
307	```
308	
309	`nestedMarkdownList` is `[Level 1, [Level 2, [Level 3]]]`.
310	
311	- **Items cannot be accessed by index.** By design there is no `myList[0]`.
312	  Piton describes things; it does not compute them, and lists exist to be
313	  merged and inherited.
314	- **A list item is never a key**, even with a colon at the end. `- Settings:`
315	  is just the string `"Settings:"`.
316	- **Anything indented under a list item is not part of that item.** It becomes
317	  the next item in the list, so a dictionary indented under an item is its own
318	  item, right after it:
319	
320	  ```piton
321	  repos:
322	      - https://github.com/piton-lang/piton-rs
323	          tag: v1
324	      - https://github.com/piton-lang/other
325	  ```
326	
327	  This compiles to
328	  `["https://github.com/piton-lang/piton-rs", {"tag": "v1"}, "https://github.com/piton-lang/other"]`.
329	  A dictionary that ends up as an item of an explicit list cannot be addressed.
330	
331	### 3.6 Dictionaries
332	
333	A dictionary has one syntax, which is indentation:
334	
335	```piton
336	firstLevel:
337	    secondLevel:
338	        thirdLevel: This is a string
339	```
340	
341	- Dot access works: `{firstLevel.secondLevel.thirdLevel}` gives
342	  `"This is a string"`.
343	- **Valid keys** contain Unicode letters, Unicode digits, `_` and `-`, and
344	  nothing else (no spaces, no dots). Keys are always strings, even when they
345	  look like something else, so `thisIsAKey`, `123`, `foo-bar`, `false` and
346	  `null` are valid keys, while `This is a key` and `a.b` are not.
347	- **A hyphen inside a name is part of the name.** `{config.foo-bar}` reads the
348	  key `foo-bar`. For subtraction, put spaces around the minus: `{a - b}`.
349	- A list indented under a key is that key's value. If the key also has
350	  something above the list, like text or another dictionary, the value becomes
351	  an implicit list (3.7) and the list goes in as one item:
352	
353	  ```piton
354	  plain:
355	      - x
356	      - y
357	  mixed:
358	      text
359	      - x
360	      - y
361	  ```
362	
363	  `plain` is `["x", "y"]`; `mixed` is `["text", ["x", "y"]]`.
364	
365	### 3.7 Implicit lists
366	
367	A block that mixes prose, list items and keys becomes an **implicit list**
368	that keeps the source order:
369	
370	```piton
371	combined:
372	    This is a string
373	
374	    - This
375	    - Is
376	    - A
377	    - List
378	
379	    nestedDictionary:
380	        deeplyNestedDictionary: This is a string
381	```
382	
383	This compiles to
384	`["This is a string", ["This", "Is", "A", "List"], {"nestedDictionary": {"deeplyNestedDictionary": "This is a string"}}]`.
385	
386	- **Keys declared directly in the mixed block stay addressable.**
387	  `{combined.nestedDictionary.deeplyNestedDictionary}` still resolves.
388	- The prose and list elements cannot be addressed, because there is no list
389	  access.
390	- An expression in running text that gives a list, dictionary or anchor also
391	  makes an implicit list (section 6.2).
392	
393	## 4. Variables and type constraints
394	
395	- A variable is declared by naming it at the top level of a file:
396	  `myVariable: 42`.
397	- The file is its scope. `export` makes it visible to other files.
398	- **Inside an expression, a plain name always means a variable from the file
399	  (or something imported), even inside an anchor.** To reach a property on the
400	  anchor you are in, use `this` or `self`:
401	
402	  ```piton
403	  x: top-level
404	
405	  anchor Card:
406	      x: card
407	      fromFile: {x}
408	      fromCard: {this.x}
409	  ```
410	
411	  `Card.fromFile` is `"top-level"` and `Card.fromCard` is `"card"`.
412	- Everything is immutable. There is no compile-time mutability.
413	
414	### 4.1 Constraint syntax
415	
416	A constraint is written `name:: type: value`. **The whitespace after `::` and
417	after `:` is mandatory**, so `myVariable::number:42` is an error
418	(`constraint-spacing`), in blocks as well as at the top level.
419	
420	```piton
421	count:: number: 42
422	tags:: string[]: [foo, bar, baz]
423	config:: dictionary:
424	    a:: number: 1
425	    b:: string: foo
426	a:: complex: [1, 2, 3]
427	c:: simple: 1
428	g:: any: 1
429	h:: any:
430	    - String
431	    - [1, 2, 3]
432	```
433	
434	- `simple` accepts string, number, boolean or null. `complex` accepts list,
435	  dictionary or anchor. `any` accepts anything.
436	- `T[]` is a list of `T`, for any type, including anchor types (`Foo[]`).
437	- `extends Foo[]` (or `extends Foo`) accepts anything that inherits from the
438	  anchor `Foo` (section 8.4). You can use it anywhere, but it is most at home
439	  in abstracts. The spec also uses it on exported lists:
440	  `export ARITHMETIC_OPERATORS:: extends ArithmeticOperator[]: ...`.
441	- An anchor-typed constraint (`f:: Foo: {Foo}`) is satisfied by the anchor or a
442	  copy of it (section 6.1).
443	- A file that names an abstract as a type must import it with
444	  `from ./Foo import Foo`. `use` alone is not enough (section 7.3).
445	
446	### 4.2 Multiple constraints and coercion
447	
448	Coercion is intentionally limited. With several constraints, they are tried
449	**left to right** and the first type the value can validly represent wins.
450	
451	```piton
452	first:: number:: string: 42
453	second:: string:: number: 42
454	written:: string: 1.0
455	evaluated:: string: {1.0}
456	quoted:: boolean:: number:: string: "false"
457	```
458	
459	- `first` is the number `42`; `second` is the string `"42"`.
460	- **A literal keeps its text when coerced to a string.** `written` is
461	  `"1.0"`. An expression is evaluated first and its result is coerced, so
462	  `evaluated` is `"1"`.
463	- `quoted` is the string `"false"`, quotes and all, because quotes are
464	  ordinary characters and `"false"` is not a boolean.
465	- **Booleans and null are never coerced**, to strings or anything else. `flag:: string: false`
466	  is a compiler error (`type-mismatch`), not the string `"false"`. If you want
467	  the string, write `${false}`.
468	- Lists, dictionaries and anchors are never coerced into unrelated types.
469	- If no constraint accepts the value, compilation fails with `type-mismatch`.
470	- These rules are about constraints. Operators such as `+` have their own
471	  rules (section 6.4).
472	
473	### 4.3 Required and optional properties
474	
475	In an abstract anchor:
476	
477	```piton
478	abstract anchor Card:
479	    title:: string
480	    subtitle:: string:: null
481	    footer:: string:: null: null
482	
483	anchor MyCard extends Card:
484	    title: Hello
485	    subtitle: null
486	```
487	
488	- A constraint with no value is **required**. Anything that extends the anchor
489	  has to give it a value (`unimplemented-property` otherwise). Adding `null` to
490	  the constraint lets that value be null, but it still has to be written, so
491	  `title` and `subtitle` are required.
492	- A property with a default value is **optional**. The usual way to write one
493	  is to allow null and default to null, like `footer`. `x:: string:: null: null`
494	  gives `null`. The language server does not complain about a missing
495	  optional property.
496	- **A child can't redeclare a constraint it inherits**, only give it a value.
497	  If `subtitle` is already constrained, `subtitle: Hi` is fine and
498	  `subtitle:: string: Hi` is `redeclared-constraint`.
499	
500	## 5. Composition lines inside blocks
501	
502	**Blocks are built from top to bottom. A line that starts with `+` or `++`
503	takes everything above it and combines it with that line's value**, using the
504	operator of the same name (section 6.4).
505	
506	```piton
507	anchor BaseAnchor:
508	    items:
509	        - A
510	        - B
511	        - C
512	
513	anchor ChildAnchor extends BaseAnchor:
514	    items:
515	        + {super.items}
516	        - D
517	        - E
518	        - F
519	```
520	
521	`ChildAnchor.items` is `[A, B, C, D, E, F]`: the block starts empty, the `+`
522	brings in `super.items`, then D, E and F are added. Without the `+`
523	(`- {super.items}`) the result is `[[A, B, C], D, E, F]`.
524	
525	- On lists, `+` merges and **removes duplicates, keeping the last
526	  occurrence**. Items `A, B, C, D` followed by `+ {super.items}` give
527	  `[D, A, B, C]`.
528	- On lists, `++` keeps everything: items `A, B, C, D` followed by
529	  `++ {super.items}` give `[A, B, C, D, A, B, C]`.
530	- On dictionaries, `+` is a shallow merge and `++` a deep merge.
531	- **On strings, `+` joins with nothing in between and `++` joins with a line
532	  break:**
533	
534	  ```piton
535	  anchor Base:
536	      d: Base text.
537	
538	  anchor Plus extends Base:
539	      d:
540	          Child text.
541	          + {super.d}
542	
543	  anchor DoublePlus extends Base:
544	      d:
545	          Child text.
546	          ++ {super.d}
547	  ```
548	
549	  `Plus.d` is `"Child text.Base text."` and `DoublePlus.d` is
550	  `"Child text.\nBase text."`.
551	- A block holding only `+ {x}` is the same as `{x}`.
552	- To put inherited prose in front with a space, interpolate instead:
553	  `${super.description} and more from the child.`
554	
555	## 6. Expressions
556	
557	**Nothing is evaluated unless it is in braces.** `a + b` is the string
558	`"a + b"`, and `{a + b}` is `3` when `a` is 1 and `b` is 2. The braces keep the
559	compiler simple, and they mean an unrecognized word never silently falls back
560	to being a string.
561	
562	- Inside the braces, **bare words are symbols**. Quote string operands:
563	  `{2 + "Hello"}` gives `"2Hello"`. An unknown name is `unresolved-symbol`.
564	  List literals inside braces follow the same rule: `{["A", "B"] + ["C"]}`.
565	- **Keep the whole expression inside the braces.** `{this.flag && false}`
566	  evaluates; `{this.flag} && false` is text around an expression.
567	- **Braces that don't hold a valid expression are an error**, and so is an
568	  empty `{}` or `${}`. To write braces as text, escape them: `\ {1 +} \`.
569	- **Forward references resolve.** Unresolved references are errors, and so are
570	  cyclic values: `A: {B}` together with `B: {A}` fails with `cyclic-value`.
571	- Collections are copied by value:
572	
573	  ```piton
574	  myList: [1, 2, 3]
575	  myDictionary:
576	      list: {myList}
577	  newList: {myDictionary.list + [4, 5, 6]}
578	  ```
579	
580	  `newList` is `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`.
581	- **Anchors are copied too, but the copy still knows which anchor it is.** If
582	  `x` is `{Foo}`, then `{x == Foo}` is `true`, `${x}` is `"Foo"`, and `x`
583	  passes a `Foo` type constraint. The output is still a copy of Foo's content.
584	  For a link instead of a copy, use `@{Foo}`.
585	
586	### 6.1 The four expression forms
587	
588	| Form | Name | Result |
589	| --- | --- | --- |
590	| `{expr}` | Standard | The intrinsic value with its type preserved. An anchor serializes as its resolved content (a copy that keeps its identity). |
591	| `${expr}` | String | Converts the result to a string. |
592	| `#{expr}` | Numeric | Converts the result to a number. |
593	| `@{expr}` | Reference | A reference to an anchor or a property on one. Renders as a link or path, never as the content. |
594	
595	Use `@{X}` to point at another document, `{X}` to embed a copy of it, and
596	`${X}` to mention it by name.
597	
598	### 6.2 Expressions in text
599	
600	If the whole value is one expression (`total: {a + b}`), it keeps its type. If
601	there is other text around it:
602	
603	- `${x}` turns the result into a string, so the whole value is a string.
604	- `{x}` with a simple value drops it into the text: `Total: {a + b}` is
605	  `"Total: 3"`.
606	- `{x}` with a list, dictionary or anchor copies it in and **turns the
607	  property into an implicit list**. `See {Foo} for details` becomes a list of
608	  `"See"`, a copy of Foo, and `"for details"`.
609	- `@{x}` puts in a reference, which ends up as a link or a path.
610	
611	### 6.3 Conversions
612	
613	`${}` (string):
614	
615	- A string is returned unchanged. A number becomes its text form. A boolean
616	  becomes `true` or `false`. Null becomes `null`.
617	- An anchor becomes its name as written in the source: `${Child}` gives
618	  `"Child"`, and `${self}` gives the name of the current most-derived anchor.
619	  It is not turned into a title.
620	- A named list or dictionary becomes its name: `Anchor.propertyName`, or just
621	  the variable name at the top of a file. So if `tags` is a top-level list,
622	  `${tags}` is `"tags"`.
623	- A list or dictionary with no name (`${[1, 2]}`) is `no-string-form`.
624	- **`${}` never pulls in the contents** of a list, dictionary or anchor, only
625	  its name. For the contents use `{x}`; for a link use `@{x}`. In
626	  `Metadata.pi`:
627	
628	  ```piton
629	  export anchor Metadata:
630	      name: Piton
631	      version:: string: 1.0
632	
633	  export byName: Information about Piton ${Metadata}
634	  export byValue: Information about Piton {Metadata}
635	  export byLink: Information about Piton @{Metadata}
636	  ```
637	
638	  `byName` is `"Information about Piton Metadata"`, `byValue` is
639	  `["Information about Piton", {"name": "Piton", "version": "1.0"}]`, and
640	  `byLink` is `"Information about Piton ./Metadata.json:Metadata"` (in
641	  Markdown, `[Metadata](./Metadata.md#metadata)`).
642	- The result is never re-parsed as source.
643	- In structured output the value stays a string; whatever escaping the output
644	  format needs is applied when it is serialized.
645	
646	`#{}` (numeric):
647	
648	- A number is returned unchanged. A string converts only if the **entire**
649	  string is a valid Piton numeric literal: `#{"42"}` gives `42`. It is never
650	  evaluated as an expression.
651	- Booleans, null, collections and anchors are rejected (`not-a-number`).
652	- The result is a number you can keep computing with. In structured output it
653	  stays numeric; it becomes text only when the output format needs text.
654	
655	### 6.4 Operators
656	
657	| Group | Operators | Rules |
658	| --- | --- | --- |
659	| Access | `.` | Property access on dictionaries and anchors. |
660	| Arithmetic | `+ - * / %` | Numbers only. Division or modulo by zero is an error. `%` keeps the sign of the left side: `{-7 % 3}` is `-1`. |
661	| Comparison | `== != < <= > >=` | The result is a boolean. `==` and `!=` work on every type (see below). `< <= > >=` work on numbers and on strings (by Unicode code point); anything else, or a number against a string, is an error. |
662	| Logical | `&& \|\| !` | Booleans only. **There is no truthiness**; anything else is `invalid-operand`. **No short-circuiting**: both sides are always evaluated and must be booleans, so `{true \|\| 5}` and `{false && 1 / 0 == 1}` are both errors. |
663	| Conditional | `cond ? a : b` | The condition must be a boolean (`invalid-condition`). Only the selected branch is evaluated. Chainable in either slot. |
664	| Concatenation / merge | `+` | Dispatches on the operand types (table below). |
665	| Duplicate merge | `++` | Lists: joined in order, duplicates kept. Dictionaries: deep merge (nested dictionaries on both sides are merged all the way down; otherwise the right side wins). Strings: joined with a line break. |
666	
667	**`+` dispatch:**
668	
669	| Left | Right | Operation |
670	| --- | --- | --- |
671	| number | number | addition |
672	| string | simple | concatenation |
673	| simple | string | concatenation |
674	| string | list, dictionary or anchor | implicit list |
675	| list, dictionary or anchor | string | implicit list |
676	| list | list | merge: joined in order, duplicates removed, last occurrence kept |
677	| dictionary | dictionary | shallow merge: keys from both, right side wins |
678	| anything else | | compiler error |
679	
680	- Concatenation stringifies the non-string side by the `${}` rules:
681	  `{2 + "Hello"}` is `"2Hello"` and `{"Enabled: " + true}` is
682	  `"Enabled: true"`.
683	- A list, dictionary or anchor is never stringified by `+`. If `tags` is
684	  `[a, b]`, `{"Tags: " + tags}` is `["Tags: ", ["a", "b"]]`. Use `${tags}` if
685	  you want the name.
686	- `{["A", "B", "C", "D"] + ["A", "B", "C"]}` is `[D, A, B, C]`;
687	  `{["A", "B", "C", "D"] ++ ["A", "B", "C"]}` is `[A, B, C, D, A, B, C]`.
688	- `{1 + true}`, `{null + 1}` and `{1 ++ 2}` are errors (`invalid-operand`).
689	
690	**Equality:** lists and dictionaries are equal if everything inside them is
691	equal. Anchors are equal only if they are the same anchor, and references only
692	if they point at the same thing.
693	
694	**Precedence** (higher rows go first; the same row goes left to right, except
695	the ternary, which goes right to left; parentheses change the order):
696	
697	| Precedence | Operators |
698	| --- | --- |
699	| 1 (highest) | `.` |
700	| 2 | `!` |
701	| 3 | `*` `/` `%` |
702	| 4 | `+` `-` `++` |
703	| 5 | `<` `<=` `>` `>=` |
704	| 6 | `==` `!=` |
705	| 7 | `&&` |
706	| 8 | `\|\|` |
707	| 9 (lowest) | `? :` |
708	
709	So `{1 + 2 == 3 && !false}` is `{((1 + 2) == 3) && (!false)}`, and
710	`{a ? b : c ? d : e}` is `{a ? b : (c ? d : e)}`.
711	
712	**Control flow:** the ternary is the only conditional, and the only operator
713	that evaluates just one side. There are no loops and no functions.
714	
715	**Declaration operators:** `:` (assignment) and `::` (type annotation) are
716	documented as operators in `spec/scope/language/operators/declaration/`
717	(`DeclarationOperators`), but they are not expression operators: they aren't in
718	`allOperators`, the precedence table, or any type's `supportedOperators`.
719	
720	**Why `+` and `++`:** on lists, `+` behaves like a set (duplicates removed,
721	last kept) and `++` like a list (duplicates kept). The spec explains this in
722	`ConcatenationOperators.setsAndLists`.
723	
724	### 6.5 References `@{}`
725	
726	- The expression must identify an anchor or **a property on one**
727	  (`@{Button}`, `@{Button.color}`). Anything else is `invalid-reference`.
728	  **A plain list or dictionary at the top of a file can't be referenced**; to
729	  link to it, put it in an anchor.
730	- The referenced anchor joins the compilation dependency graph (for a
731	  property, the anchor it is on), so it gets compiled and emitted.
732	- References are resolved separately for each output target, through the
733	  renderer or the framework adapter on top of it. If a target cannot represent
734	  a reference, that is an error. A reference never silently becomes an
735	  embedded copy or a plain name.
736	- References compare with `==` and `!=`: equal if they point at the same
737	  thing.
738	- How each renderer writes one:
739	
740	  | Renderer | Reference to `Button` | Reference to `Button.color` |
741	  | --- | --- | --- |
742	  | JSON | `"./Button.json:Button"` | `"./Button.json:Button.color"` |
743	  | YAML | `./Button.yaml:Button` | `./Button.yaml:Button.color` |
744	  | Markdown | `[Button](./Button.md#button)` | `[Button.color](./Button.md#color)` |
745	
746	  JSON and YAML write the path to the other output file (relative to this
747	  one), a colon, and the dot path. Markdown writes a relative link with the
748	  anchor's name (or `Anchor.property`) as the link text, and a fragment for the
749	  specific anchor or property heading. The link is **lazy**: the content is
750	  not inlined, and an agent follows it only when the work touches what it
751	  describes.
752	- A Markdown link you write yourself (`[Button](./Button.md)`) is plain text,
753	  not a reference. Only `@{...}` is resolved and checked.
754	
755	## 7. Modules and reuse
756	
757	### 7.1 Export and import
758	
759	```piton
760	export pi: 3.14
761	myVariable: 42
762	export anchor MyAnchor:
763	    description: This is my anchor
764	```
765	
766	`myVariable` is not exported, so no other file can import it.
767	
768	```piton
769	from ./FirstFile import pi, MyAnchor
770	from ./FirstFile import pi SliceOf, MyAnchor MyAliasedAnchor
771	from /subdir/subdir/file import AnAnchor
772	from ./path/to/directory import MyAnchor
773	from .. import Something
774	from my-package import MyAnchor
775	from @piton/belay import ClaudeCodeAdapter
776	from ./file import
777	    FirstThing,
778	    SecondThing,
779	    ThirdThing
780	```
781	
782	- Paths are relative to the current file. A path that starts with `/` is
783	  relative to the `root` in `piton.config.pi`.
784	- **The `.pi` extension is optional**, and `piton format` removes it.
785	- A bare `.` or `..` points at the `index.pi` in that directory. A directory
786	  path resolves to its `index.pi`.
787	- Only exported names can be imported (`unresolved-export`). A missing module
788	  is `unresolved-module`.
789	- Aliasing is `Name Alias`, with no `as`. After aliasing, only the alias is in
790	  scope (`pi` above is available only as `SliceOf`).
791	- `export Name` on its own line re-exports something already declared or
792	  imported.
793	- **Circular imports are allowed.** Mutually referencing values are fine as
794	  long as every value settles:
795	
796	  ```piton
797	  anchor A:
798	      description: This anchor talks about ${B}
799	
800	  anchor B:
801	      description: This anchor talks about ${A}
802	  ```
803	
804	  This works because both settle to strings (the anchor names). `A: {B}` with
805	  `B: {A}` cannot resolve, so it fails. The only cycles that are errors are
806	  ones that can't resolve and an anchor that ends up extending itself.
807	
808	### 7.2 Index files and re-export
809	
810	An `index.pi` file exposes a directory as a module:
811	
812	```piton
813	from ./MyAnchor import MyAnchor
814	export MyAnchor
815	```
816	
817	The shorter forms:
818	
819	```piton
820	from ./MyAnchor export MyAnchor
821	from ./MyAnchor export *
822	from ./MyAnchor export MyAnchor MyAliasedAnchor, MyOtherAnchor MyOtherAliasedAnchor
823	```
824	
825	**Importing a name into an index does not re-export it.** When an index uses
826	`import`, consumers must import leaf anchors from their own files, or the
827	index must `export` them.
828	
829	### 7.3 `use`
830	
831	`use` brings the **user-defined keywords** a module exports into scope, and
832	nothing else. `from ... import` never brings keywords.
833	
834	```piton
835	use ./CustomKeywords
836	
837	my-custom-keyword Wow:
838	    description: amazing
839	```
840	
841	- Valid forms include `use ./CustomKeywords`, `use .`, `use ../cli`,
842	  `use my-package`, `use my-package/MyAnchor` and `use @piton/belay`.
843	- A file that declares with a keyword *and* names its abstract as a type needs
844	  both lines: `use ./Foo` and `from ./Foo import Foo`.
845	- Using a keyword without `use` gives `unknown-keyword`.
846	
847	### 7.4 Formatting of imports
848	
849	`piton format` sorts the imports: in each run of import lines, the `use`
850	lines come first, then the `from` lines, each sorted by path, and the names in
851	each line are sorted too. A blank line keeps two runs apart. It breaks an
852	import or `from ... export` line across lines when it has more than 2 items or
853	runs past 80 columns, and drops the `.pi` extension from paths. You can write
854	those line breaks yourself on either kind of line.
855	
856	## 8. Anchors
857	
858	An anchor is a named structural declaration that can take part in
859	inheritance, typing, exports and composition. It is the core building block of
860	Piton, something like a class that is never instantiated. An *object* is a
861	value. An *anchor* is a declaration.
